question: How do I add a max length validation to an optional query parameter in FastAPI?
reference_answer: Import Query from fastapi and Annotated from typing, then declare the parameter as q: Annotated[str | None, Query(max_length=50)] = None. FastAPI will validate that the value doesn't exceed 50 characters, show a clear error to the client when invalid, and document the constraint in the OpenAPI schema. Annotated support requires FastAPI 0.95.0 or later (upgrade to at least 0.95.1).

question: Can I set a default value inside Query() when I'm also using Annotated?
reference_answer: No - when using Query inside Annotated you cannot use the default parameter of Query, because it would be ambiguous which default wins. Instead, set the actual default value on the function parameter, e.g. q: Annotated[str, Query()] = "rick". The Query(default=...) style is only for the old, non-Annotated syntax.

question: How do I require a path parameter to be a number greater than or equal to 1 and less than or equal to 1000?
reference_answer: Use Path from fastapi with numeric constraint arguments, e.g. item_id: Annotated[int, Path(ge=1, le=1000)]. The available numeric validations are gt (greater than), ge (greater than or equal), lt (less than), and le (less than or equal), and they also work for float values.

question: Does setting a default value or None on a path parameter make it optional?
reference_answer: No. A path parameter is always required because it has to be part of the path - even if you declare it with None or give it a default value, that doesn't change anything and it remains required.

question: I have a single Pydantic model body parameter, but I want the JSON to be wrapped under a key like {"item": {...}} instead of the model fields at the top level. How do I do that?
reference_answer: Use the embed parameter of Body: declare the parameter as item: Annotated[Item, Body(embed=True)]. FastAPI will then expect the JSON body to have an "item" key with the model's contents inside it, instead of expecting the model attributes directly at the top level.

question: How can I add a singular value like an integer 'importance' field to the request body alongside my Pydantic model parameters?
reference_answer: Declare it with Body, e.g. importance: Annotated[int, Body()]. Without Body, FastAPI would assume a singular value is a query parameter; with it, FastAPI treats it as another key in the JSON body next to the other body parameters.

question: Where do I import Field from to add validation to attributes inside a Pydantic model?
reference_answer: Field is imported directly from pydantic, not from fastapi - unlike Query, Path, and Body, which come from fastapi. Field works the same way as those and accepts all the same validation and metadata parameters for model attributes.

question: How do I make a query parameter optional in FastAPI?
reference_answer: Declare the function parameter with a default value of None, e.g. q: str | None = None. FastAPI treats it as an optional query parameter that will be None if the client does not provide it, while parameters without any default value are required.

question: Which values in the URL does FastAPI accept as True for a bool query parameter?
reference_answer: For a parameter declared as bool, values like 1, True, true, on, and yes (in any case variation, e.g. uppercase or first letter capitalized) are all converted to True; anything else is converted to False.

question: I have routes /users/me and /users/{user_id} - why does /users/me get treated as a user_id, and how do I fix it?
reference_answer: Path operations are evaluated in the order they are declared, so /users/{user_id} declared first will also match /users/me, receiving user_id="me". You must declare the fixed path /users/me before the parameterized /users/{user_id}.

question: How can I declare a path parameter that itself contains a path with slashes, like a file path?
reference_answer: Use Starlette's path convertor in the route, e.g. /files/{file_path:path} - the :path suffix makes the parameter match any path including slashes. Note OpenAPI doesn't support this, so the docs won't document that the parameter should contain a path; for a leading slash the URL will contain a double slash, like /files//home/johndoe/myfile.txt.

question: How do I declare a JSON request body for a POST endpoint in FastAPI?
reference_answer: Import BaseModel from pydantic, create a class inheriting from BaseModel with attributes declared using standard Python types, and declare a function parameter of that model type in the path operation (e.g. item: Item). FastAPI will read the body as JSON, convert and validate the data, and pass it in that parameter.

question: When I mix body, path, and query parameters in one endpoint, how does FastAPI decide which function parameter comes from where?
reference_answer: If a parameter is also declared in the path it is taken as a path parameter; if it is a singular type (int, float, str, bool, etc.) it is interpreted as a query parameter; if it is typed as a Pydantic model it is interpreted as the request body. Also note FastAPI decides a parameter is not required because of the default value = None, not because of the str | None annotation.

question: What command do I run to install FastAPI with all the standard optional dependencies?
reference_answer: Run pip install "fastapi[standard]" inside an activated virtual environment. This includes optional standard dependencies such as fastapi-cloud-cli; use pip install fastapi for a minimal install, or pip install "fastapi[standard-no-fastapi-cloud-cli]" to get the standard extras without the cloud CLI.

question: How do I stop FastAPI from including fields with default values in my JSON responses when they weren't actually set?
reference_answer: Set the path operation decorator parameter response_model_exclude_unset=True; then only values that were explicitly set are included in the response, not the model's defaults. Related options are response_model_exclude_defaults=True and response_model_exclude_none=True.

question: If I declare both a return type annotation and a response_model on the same path operation, which one does FastAPI use?
reference_answer: The response_model parameter takes priority over the return type annotation. This lets you keep an accurate return type for editors and mypy while FastAPI uses response_model for validation, documentation, and filtering; you can also pass response_model=None to disable response model generation entirely.

question: Why can't I write response_model=PlaneItem | CarItem in Python 3.10, when the | syntax normally works for unions?
reference_answer: Because response_model is passed as a value to an argument rather than used in a type annotation, Python would try to actually perform an invalid operation between the two classes. You must use typing.Union instead, e.g. response_model=Union[PlaneItem, CarItem], putting the most specific type first.

question: How do I return a 404 error with a custom message when an item doesn't exist in FastAPI?
reference_answer: Import HTTPException from fastapi and raise it (don't return it), e.g. raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Item not found"). The client receives a 404 response with a JSON body {"detail": "Item not found"}, and the detail parameter can be any JSON-convertible value such as a dict or list, not only a string.

question: When I add a custom exception handler for HTTP errors, should I register it for FastAPI's HTTPException or Starlette's?
reference_answer: Register the handler for Starlette's HTTPException (e.g. imported as StarletteHTTPException) so it also catches exceptions raised by Starlette's internal code, extensions, or plug-ins, while you keep raising FastAPI's HTTPException in your own code. The only difference between the two classes is that FastAPI's HTTPException accepts any JSON-able data for detail while Starlette's only accepts strings.

question: I need to store a Pydantic model with a datetime field in a database that only accepts JSON-compatible data. What does FastAPI offer for this?
reference_answer: Use FastAPI's jsonable_encoder() function: it takes an object like a Pydantic model and returns a JSON-compatible version, converting the model to a dict and datetime objects to ISO-format strings. It returns a standard Python data structure (not a JSON string) that can then be encoded with json.dumps().

question: How do I implement partial updates with PATCH in FastAPI so that fields the client didn't send don't get overwritten with defaults?
reference_answer: Call item.model_dump(exclude_unset=True) on the input model to get a dict containing only the fields actually sent in the request, then apply it to the stored model with stored_item_model.model_copy(update=update_data). Note the input model must have all attributes marked optional (with defaults or None) so clients can omit fields, and the same technique also works with PUT.

question: Why do I need to pass check_same_thread=False when creating a SQLite engine for my FastAPI app?
reference_answer: Setting check_same_thread=False in connect_args allows FastAPI to use the same SQLite database in different threads, which is necessary because a single request could use more than one thread (for example in dependencies). It is safe because the app is structured to use a single SQLModel Session per request.

question: How do I build a PATCH endpoint that only updates the fields the client actually sent, ignoring unset defaults?
reference_answer: Use an update data model (e.g. HeroUpdate) where all fields are optional with a default of None, then call hero.model_dump(exclude_unset=True) to get a dict containing only the data the client actually sent, and apply it to the database object with hero_db.sqlmodel_update(hero_data).

question: When I set a prefix on an APIRouter, should the prefix end with a slash?
reference_answer: No - the prefix must not include a final /. Since each path operation's path has to start with / (e.g. @router.get("/{item_id}")), the prefix should be written like /items so combined paths become /items/ and /items/{item_id}.

question: How can I tell the fastapi command where my app object lives so I don't have to pass the file path every time?
reference_answer: Configure the entrypoint in pyproject.toml under a [tool.fastapi] section, e.g. entrypoint = "app.main:app", which is equivalent to importing 'from app.main import app'. This is recommended over passing the path (fastapi dev app/main.py) each time, and it also lets tools like the VS Code extension and FastAPI Cloud find your app.

question: Do my test functions need to be async def when using FastAPI's TestClient?
reference_answer: No - test functions should be normal def, not async def, and calls to the TestClient are normal calls without await, which lets you use pytest directly without complications. Note you must install httpx first to use TestClient, and test function names should start with test_ per the pytest convention.

question: What's the difference between BackgroundTasks and BackgroundTask in FastAPI, and which one should I import?
reference_answer: Import BackgroundTasks (with the 's') from fastapi and declare it as a path operation function parameter - FastAPI creates the object and handles running the tasks for you. BackgroundTask (without the 's') comes from starlette.background and, if used, requires you to create the object yourself and return a Starlette Response that includes it.

question: How do I completely disable the OpenAPI schema and the interactive docs for my FastAPI app?
reference_answer: Set openapi_url=None when creating the FastAPI app, which disables the OpenAPI schema (served at /openapi.json by default) and also disables the documentation UIs that depend on it. You can also individually disable Swagger UI with docs_url=None and ReDoc with redoc_url=None.

question: What's the advantage of using UploadFile instead of bytes for file uploads in FastAPI?
reference_answer: UploadFile uses a spooled file that is kept in memory only up to a size limit and then stored on disk, so it works well for large files without consuming all memory. It also gives you metadata (filename, content_type), a file-like async interface with methods like write, read, seek, and close, and exposes an actual SpooledTemporaryFile you can pass to other libraries. With bytes, the whole file content is loaded into memory, which only works well for small files.

question: Can I receive both form fields and a JSON body in the same FastAPI endpoint?
reference_answer: No. You can declare multiple Form parameters in a path operation, but you can't also declare Body fields expected as JSON, because the request body will be encoded as application/x-www-form-urlencoded instead of application/json. This is a limitation of the HTTP protocol, not of FastAPI.

question: What are the default values for allow_methods and allow_credentials in FastAPI's CORSMiddleware?
reference_answer: CORSMiddleware is restrictive by default: allow_methods defaults to ['GET'] and allow_credentials defaults to False (allow_headers defaults to [] and max_age defaults to 600 seconds). Also, if allow_credentials is set to True, none of allow_origins, allow_methods, or allow_headers can be set to ['*'] - they must be explicitly specified.

question: If I add multiple middlewares to my FastAPI app, in what order do they run?
reference_answer: Each new middleware wraps the application, forming a stack: the last middleware added is the outermost and runs first on the request path and last on the response path. For example, after app.add_middleware(MiddlewareA) then app.add_middleware(MiddlewareB), the request flows MiddlewareB -> MiddlewareA -> route, and the response flows route -> MiddlewareA -> MiddlewareB.

question: How do I write a FastAPI middleware that adds a header with the request processing time?
reference_answer: Use the @app.middleware("http") decorator on a function that receives the request and a call_next function; call response = await call_next(request), then set a custom header like X-Process-Time on the response before returning it. The docs recommend measuring the time with time.perf_counter() instead of time.time() because it is more precise.

question: How can I read a header like User-Agent that has a hyphen in its name, since that's not a valid Python variable name?
reference_answer: Declare the parameter with Header using snake_case, e.g. user_agent: str | None = Header(default=None) - by default Header converts underscores to hyphens to extract and document the header, and HTTP headers are case-insensitive. If you need to disable this, set convert_underscores=False, but beware that some HTTP proxies and servers disallow headers with underscores.

question: Why don't my cookie values show up when I test a cookie parameter from the Swagger UI at /docs?
reference_answer: Browsers handle cookies specially and don't easily allow JavaScript to touch them, and since the docs UI at /docs works with JavaScript, the cookies won't be sent even if you fill in the values and click Execute - you'll see an error as if no values were provided. The cookie parameter itself is declared with Cookie, the same way as Query and Path parameters.

question: Why should I use the exec form of CMD instead of the shell form in my FastAPI Dockerfile?
reference_answer: Use the exec form, e.g. CMD ["fastapi", "run", "app/main.py", "--port", "80"], because it ensures FastAPI can shut down gracefully and lifespan events are triggered. With the shell form (CMD fastapi run ...) this doesn't happen, which is noticeable with docker compose where services can take about 10 seconds to stop.

question: In my Dockerfile, why should I copy requirements.txt and install dependencies before copying the rest of my app code?
reference_answer: Docker builds images in layers and caches each step; requirements.txt changes rarely, so copying it alone first lets Docker reuse the cached layer for the COPY and the pip install step (RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --upgrade -r /code/requirements.txt). The app code changes most frequently, so COPY ./app goes near the end-otherwise every code change would invalidate the cache and re-download all dependencies, turning seconds-long builds into minutes.

question: How can a single server with one IP address serve HTTPS for multiple domains with different certificates?
reference_answer: Through the SNI (Server Name Indication) extension to the TLS protocol, which lets one server with a single IP address hold several HTTPS certificates and serve multiple HTTPS domains. For this to work, a single component (typically the TLS Termination Proxy) listening on the public IP must have all the HTTPS certificates on the server.

question: My FastAPI app is behind a reverse proxy that terminates HTTPS. How do I make the server trust the X-Forwarded headers the proxy sends?
reference_answer: By default the application server doesn't trust the X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto, and X-Forwarded-Host headers. With FastAPI CLI, use the --forwarded-allow-ips option to specify the IPs to trust; if the server only receives traffic from the trusted proxy you can set --forwarded-allow-ips="*" to trust all incoming IPs.

question: How do I start my FastAPI app with multiple worker processes to use all my CPU cores?
reference_answer: Use the --workers command line option, e.g. fastapi run --workers 4 main.py, or with Uvicorn directly: uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 --workers 4. This starts a parent process acting as the process manager plus one server process per worker.

question: What does the 'main:app' part mean when I run 'uvicorn main:app'?
reference_answer: main refers to the file main.py (the Python module) and app is the FastAPI object created inside it with app = FastAPI(). The import string is equivalent to the Python statement 'from main import app'.

question: Should I pin the Starlette and Pydantic versions in my FastAPI project's requirements?
reference_answer: Do not pin starlette-each FastAPI version uses a specific newer Starlette version, so let FastAPI choose it. Pydantic can be pinned to any version above 1.0.0 that works for you (e.g. pydantic>=2.7.0,<3.0.0), since new Pydantic versions are always kept compatible with FastAPI.

question: How do I return an HTTP redirect from a FastAPI endpoint, and what status code does it use by default?
reference_answer: Use RedirectResponse, either by returning it directly or by setting it as the response_class in the path operation decorator (in which case you can just return the URL). By default it uses the 307 Temporary Redirect status code, and you can change it with the status_code parameter.

question: If I return a Response object directly from my path operation function, will it still show up in the automatic docs?
reference_answer: No - a Response returned directly is not documented in OpenAPI (its Content-Type won't be documented) and won't appear in the interactive docs. To document the media type while still returning a Response, pass the response class via the response_class parameter AND return the Response object; response_class is then used only for documentation.

question: How do I run startup and shutdown code in FastAPI, like loading an ML model before requests and releasing it afterwards?
reference_answer: Define an async function with yield decorated with @asynccontextmanager and pass it to the FastAPI app via the lifespan parameter. Code before the yield runs once before the app starts receiving requests, and code after the yield runs after it finishes handling requests, at shutdown.

question: Can I use both the lifespan parameter and the old @app.on_event startup/shutdown handlers in the same FastAPI app?
reference_answer: No. If you provide a lifespan parameter, the startup and shutdown event handlers will no longer be called - it's all lifespan or all events, not both. The startup/shutdown events are deprecated and lifespan is the recommended approach.

question: How do I avoid re-reading my .env file on every request when using a Pydantic Settings dependency in FastAPI?
reference_answer: Decorate the get_settings() dependency function with @lru_cache (from functools), so the Settings object is created only once on the first call and the same cached object is returned for subsequent requests. Because it's still a dependency, you can override it easily in tests via a dependency override for get_settings.

question: What are the configuration options for GZipMiddleware in FastAPI and what are their defaults?
reference_answer: GZipMiddleware supports minimum_size (responses smaller than this size in bytes are not gzipped, default 500) and compresslevel (an integer from 1 to 9, default 9, where lower values compress faster but produce larger output). It compresses responses for requests that include "gzip" in the Accept-Encoding header and handles both standard and streaming responses.

question: How can I detect when a client disconnects from a WebSocket in FastAPI?
reference_answer: When the WebSocket connection is closed, the await websocket.receive_text() call raises a WebSocketDisconnect exception, which you can catch (e.g. in a try/except) to handle the disconnect, such as removing the client from a connection list and broadcasting a message to the other clients.

question: I have a dependency with yield - can I make FastAPI run its cleanup code before the response is sent instead of after?
reference_answer: Yes, use Depends(scope="function"), which closes the dependency after the path operation function returns but before the response is sent to the client. The other option is scope="request", which runs the exit code after the response is sent, and that is the default when a dependency with yield does not specify a scope.

question: In my dependency with yield I catch exceptions with except so my endpoint doesn't blow up - is that okay?
reference_answer: No - if you catch an exception in a dependency with yield and don't re-raise it, FastAPI can't notice it: the client still gets an HTTP 500 Internal Server Error, but the server will have no logs or any indication of what the error was. Unless you are raising an HTTPException or similar instead, you should re-raise the original exception with raise.

question: When using a class as a dependency, do I really have to write the class name twice, like commons: Annotated[CommonQueryParams, Depends(CommonQueryParams)]?
reference_answer: No - FastAPI provides a shortcut for the case where the dependency is specifically a class it will call to create an instance: declare the class as the type annotation and use Depends() with no argument, e.g. commons: Annotated[CommonQueryParams, Depends()]. FastAPI extracts the dependency from the type annotation itself.

question: What does OAuth2PasswordBearer actually do when a request comes in without an Authorization header?
reference_answer: OAuth2PasswordBearer looks in the request for the Authorization header and checks that its value is "Bearer " plus a token, returning the token as a str. If the header is missing or doesn't contain a Bearer token, it responds directly with a 401 UNAUTHORIZED status code error, so your function is only executed when a token string is present.

question: Why does my OAuth2 password login example fail with an error about form data - do I need to install something extra?
reference_answer: OAuth2 sends the username and password as form data, which requires the python-multipart package. It is installed automatically with pip install "fastapi[standard]", but if you installed with plain pip install fastapi it is not included and you must install it manually with pip install python-multipart.

question: How do I generate the secret key for signing JWT tokens in FastAPI, and which algorithm should I use?
reference_answer: Generate a secure random secret key with the command openssl rand -hex 32 and copy the output into the SECRET_KEY variable (don't reuse the example's key). Then create an ALGORITHM variable set to "HS256" for signing the JWT tokens; the docs use the PyJWT package (pip install pyjwt) to generate and verify them.

question: What security scheme types does OpenAPI define that I can use with FastAPI?
reference_answer: OpenAPI defines four security scheme types: apiKey (a key from a query parameter, header, or cookie), http (standard HTTP auth like bearer, HTTP Basic, and HTTP Digest), oauth2 (the OAuth2 flows such as implicit, clientCredentials, authorizationCode, and password), and openIdConnect (automatic discovery of OAuth2 authentication data). FastAPI provides tools for these schemes in the fastapi.security module.

question: My FastAPI app is behind an Nginx/Traefik proxy that strips the /api/v1 path prefix, and now the /docs UI can't load the OpenAPI schema. How do I fix this?
reference_answer: Tell FastAPI about the stripped prefix by starting the server with the --root-path option, e.g. `fastapi run main.py --forwarded-allow-ips="*" --root-path /api/v1`, or equivalently pass root_path="/api/v1" when creating the FastAPI app. FastAPI then uses that root_path to create the default server entry in the OpenAPI schema so the docs UI fetches the schema from the correct prefixed URL.

question: I'm passing my own servers list to FastAPI, but it keeps inserting an extra server based on root_path at the start of the list. How do I turn that off?
reference_answer: Set the parameter root_path_in_servers=False when creating the FastAPI app. By default, when you pass a custom servers list and a root_path exists, FastAPI inserts a server with the root_path URL at the beginning of the list; this parameter prevents it from being included in the OpenAPI schema.

question: How do I require an OAuth2 scope like "items" on a specific FastAPI endpoint?
reference_answer: Import Security from fastapi and use it instead of Depends in the path operation, passing the dependency function plus a scopes parameter with a list of scope strings, e.g. Security(get_current_active_user, scopes=["items"]). In the underlying dependency you can declare a parameter of type SecurityScopes (from fastapi.security), whose .scopes property lists all scopes required by the path operation and its dependency tree, so you can verify the token contains them.

question: Why does FastAPI's HTTP Basic Auth example use secrets.compare_digest() instead of just comparing the username and password with ==?
reference_answer: A plain == comparison short-circuits at the first differing character, so response times leak how many leading characters an attacker guessed correctly, enabling a timing attack that can recover credentials character by character. secrets.compare_digest() takes the same time regardless of how much of the strings match, protecting against this. Note it requires bytes or ASCII-only strings, so the docs encode the username and password to UTF-8 bytes first.

question: How can I completely disable the /docs and /openapi.json endpoints in production with FastAPI?
reference_answer: Declare a Pydantic setting like openapi_url (defaulting to "/openapi.json") and pass it as the openapi_url parameter to the FastAPI app, then set the environment variable to an empty string (e.g. `OPENAPI_URL= uvicorn main:app`). With openapi_url empty, /openapi.json, /docs, and /redoc all return a 404 Not Found. The docs warn this is security through obscurity and shouldn't be your way of protecting the API.

question: Which GraphQL library is recommended for use with FastAPI, and what other options are there?
reference_answer: Strawberry is the recommended library because its design is closest to FastAPI's, being based on type annotations. Other ASGI-compatible options include Ariadne, Tartiflette (with tartiflette-asgi), and Graphene (with starlette-graphene3); the old GraphQLApp from Starlette is deprecated and code using it should migrate to starlette-graphene3.

question: Is there a tool that can automatically migrate my FastAPI app's models from Pydantic v1 to Pydantic v2?
reference_answer: Yes, use bump-pydantic, a tool from the Pydantic team that automatically changes most of the code that needs updating when you use regular Pydantic models without customizations. After running it, run your test suite to confirm everything still works; if bump-pydantic isn't enough, FastAPI 0.119.0 to 0.127.x temporarily allowed mixing pydantic.v1 and v2 models in the same app for gradual migration, but that support was removed in FastAPI 0.128.0.

question: My path operation function only does a small computation and no I/O at all - should I declare it with def or async def?
reference_answer: Use async def. In FastAPI, path operation functions declared with plain def are run in an external threadpool that is then awaited, so for trivial compute-only functions the tiny performance gain you might expect from def in other frameworks is reversed. Use plain def only when the function performs blocking I/O.

question: When I use Annotated on a parameter, which part does Python treat as the real type?
reference_answer: The first type parameter passed to Annotated is the actual type; everything after it is just metadata for other tools (like FastAPI). Annotated is imported from the standard typing module, and Python itself does nothing with the metadata - for editors the type is still e.g. str.

question: What does os.getenv return if the environment variable I'm asking for isn't set?
reference_answer: It returns the second argument, which is the default value - for example os.getenv("MY_NAME", "World") returns "World". If no default is provided, it returns None. Also note that any value read from an environment variable is always a str, so type conversion and validation must be done in code.

question: What does activating a Python virtual environment actually do under the hood?
reference_answer: Activating (e.g. with source .venv/bin/activate on Linux/macOS or .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 in PowerShell) modifies environment variables, most importantly prepending the virtual environment's path (.venv/bin on Linux/macOS, .venv\Scripts on Windows) to the beginning of the PATH variable. Because it comes first, running python finds the interpreter from the virtual environment before any global Python.

question: What's the difference between running my app with fastapi dev versus fastapi run?
reference_answer: fastapi dev starts development mode: auto-reload is enabled by default and the server listens only on 127.0.0.1 (localhost). fastapi run is for production: auto-reload is disabled and it listens on 0.0.0.0, making it publicly accessible; internally both use Uvicorn.

question: How do I tell the fastapi CLI where my app object is without passing the path on every command?
reference_answer: Set the entrypoint in pyproject.toml under [tool.fastapi], e.g. entrypoint = "backend.main:app", which tells the fastapi command to import the app as 'from backend.main import app'. You can alternatively pass a file path (fastapi dev main.py) or the --entrypoint option (fastapi dev --entrypoint main:app), but the pyproject.toml approach is recommended so other tools like the VS Code extension can also find the app.

question: Benchmarks show Starlette and Uvicorn beating FastAPI - why is FastAPI slower, and what should I actually compare it against?
reference_answer: FastAPI is built on Starlette, which runs on Uvicorn, so it cannot be faster than either - it executes their code plus extra features like data validation and serialization. Comparing them as equivalents is misleading: Uvicorn should be compared against other servers (Daphne, Hypercorn, uWSGI), Starlette against web frameworks (Sanic, Flask, Django), and FastAPI against frameworks with integrated validation, serialization, and documentation such as Flask-apispec, NestJS, or Molten.
